title: Son of encouragement (Acts 4:23–37)
hookLine: a Cypriot named Joseph sells a field and is nicknamed Barnabas, son of encouragement
tomorrow: another couple sells land too. why does their story end so hard?

cards: Nicknames say what people really think of you: the one who's always late, the one who always has snacks.

Acts gives a man a nickname and stops to translate it: "Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus."
Today's title says encouragement; the King James says consolation, comfort that puts strength back in.
And his first act on the page is quiet: "Having land, sold it, and brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet."

teach.b: He lives in a community Acts describes as "of one heart and of one soul," where "Neither was there any among them that lacked." And the name sticks because people see what he's like.

Acts isn't finished with Barnabas, though, and later it shows what being one can cost. Barnabas and Paul plan a journey. Barnabas wants to bring John Mark, who had left them partway through an earlier trip.
And Acts says "the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other." Two good men, one real argument, and Christians have taken both sides.
Paul's best case: the work is hard and dangerous, trust is earned, and setting someone up to fail again isn't kind to him or to the people depending on him.
Barnabas's best case: people grow when someone believes in them, and a second chance is exactly what a son of consolation is for. Acts doesn't call either man wrong. It lets them go two ways.
One to tell a friend tonight: later, in a letter that bears Paul's name, he asks for Mark by name: "he is profitable to me for the ministry."
The one Barnabas wouldn't give up on turned out to be worth it. That doesn't settle every case. It does show why the nickname mattered.

how: Some churches keep a feast day for Saint Barnabas, and some Christians call a person who encourages others 'a Barnabas'.

games.why: Acts tells the split over Mark without ranking Paul or Barnabas. later, a letter bearing Paul's name calls Mark profitable for the ministry.
